tagline: River bends through replanted forest lead to a lighthouse headland.
intro: Trees to Sea crosses the Oregon Coast Range on a drive of river bends, forest and dairy pasture before reaching the Pacific. Travel Oregon presents the designated byway as a 68-mile journey through forests to a rocky headland, with two to three hours of driving. OR 6 brings numerous turns and steep grades through the mountains.

Works Progress Administration crews helped build the road during the Great Depression. Before 1957, OR 6 ran through Gales Creek and the Tualatin Valley into Portland. Completion of the Sunset Highway and the new Banks alignment shifted OR 6 to its present route; the former approach became OR 8. Along that crossing, the Tillamook Burn had begun in 1933 near Gales Creek Overlook. Replanting later brought millions of seedlings to the burned forest.

Begin at Banks, where farms and vineyards meet the rising Coast Range, and follow OR 6 west into Tillamook State Forest near Gales Creek Overlook. The road twists beside the Devils Lake Fork of the Wilson River, passing the Tillamook Forest Center before descending into dairy pasture. At Tillamook, the route crosses US 101 and continues west on OR 131 to Netarts Bay. It then turns north along the coast through Oceanside to Cape Meares, where the lighthouse marks the point.

moments.title: Tillamook Forest Center
moments.text: A 40-foot replica fire lookout marks the Tillamook Forest Center entrance. Inside, exhibits explain how Oregonians replanted the Tillamook Burn. The work combined a billion Douglas-fir seeds dropped from helicopters with more than 72 million seedlings planted by hand between 1949 and 1972. Governor Tom McCall designated the Burn a state forest in 1973. Behind the center, a suspension bridge crosses the Wilson River and connects with the Wilson River trail. The Oregon Department of Forestry manages this public forest for recreation and commercial activities, including timber harvesting and mushroom gathering.

moments.title: Oceanside
moments.text: Three Arch Rocks lies offshore from Oceanside, with three large rocky islands and six smaller ones. William L. Finley and Herman Bohlman began studying and photographing the rocks from here in 1901. They documented hunters killing sea lions for skin and oil and shooting seabirds for sport. Their campaign persuaded Theodore Roosevelt to establish a wildlife refuge in 1907. The rocks support breeding tufted puffins and common murres; the byway offers views from Oceanside. Congress designated the refuge wilderness in 1970. Its protected islands also provide a breeding site for Steller sea lions.

moments.title: Cape Meares
moments.text: Four sides of the lighthouse’s eight-sided lens carried red glass, producing alternating red and white beams as it turned. The old light was deactivated in 1963 and replaced by a newer tower. Plans to demolish it the next year fell through after public protest, and the Coast Guard transferred the station to Tillamook County. The state scenic viewpoint includes both the lighthouse and the Octopus Tree. A short hike from the main parking lot reaches that multi-trunked Sitka spruce. The cape forms a high, steep bluff at the south end of Tillamook Bay, with Short Beach immediately to its south.
